old: The structural analogy is precise rather than loose. A Norwegian patient summary moving from a Norwegian National Contact Point for eHealth to a Spanish point of care is a digital good crossing a jurisdictional boundary. It must satisfy the originating jurisdiction's audit and retention rules, the destination jurisdiction's clinical and consent rules, and any superordinate Union-level provisions. The audit log of the cross-border access event is the digital equivalent of the customs documentation that accompanies physical goods. The retention floor on that audit log is the digital equivalent of customs record-keeping. The Union Customs Code requires the person concerned to keep the documents and information on which a customs declaration rests "for at least three years", the period running from the end of the year in which the declaration is accepted or the procedure discharged, and extended while a correction, an appeal or court proceedings are pending (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2013, Article 51). The erasure obligation of Article 17 GDPR has its physical counterpart in destruction: customs authorities "may require goods which have been presented to customs to be destroyed" (Article 197). The two do not collide, because destruction reaches the goods and record-keeping reaches the documents, so the record of a destroyed consignment, including the fact of its destruction, is kept for the full period. That separation of the record from the thing recorded is what Semantics II does for the audit trail, where accountability attaches to the record of the access and of its payload's invalidation rather than to the payload's continued existence (Chapter 4, Section 4.5). Checked against the anchoring result of Chapter 6, Section 6.9a, the customs case confirms it from the other side: the destruction power is anchored to an external event, a customs decision, and would cross the record-keeping floor if it reached the documents; it does not, because it is confined to the goods. The analogy also marks where it stops. In customs the floor and the destruction act on different objects by design, whereas in an audit trail the personal data and the record of their processing begin in the same record, and the mechanism has to separate them.

old: The limitation concerns profiles rather than versions. Synthea's default export conforms to the US Core implementation guide and draws its demographic, geographic, and care-pattern parameters from a United States population. The FHIR version therefore matches the version Norwegian basisprofiler constrain, but the profiles and the clinical content do not represent Norwegian practice, and this thesis makes no claim that they do. The consequence is bounded and is verified rather than assumed in Chapter 5, Section 5.7: because no constraint in the model reads the content of a payload, the demonstration's results are invariant to payload provenance, and Norwegian representativeness is required of the *infrastructure analysis* in Chapter 4 rather than of the generated records.

old: The *feasibility checker* is the primary layer and the executable witness of the propositions. It constructs audit records as the tuples defined in Chapter 4, Section 4.3, in two classes: cross-border audit records carrying the ten-year floor, and Secure Processing Environment access-log records carrying the one-year floor and the six-month ceiling. It then generates randomised arrivals of erasure requests and permit expiries across a monthly time horizon, and evaluates the three constraints under each semantics in turn, reporting violations. The two classes differ only in their floor parameter and in whether the ceiling applies, which is what makes them instances of one model rather than two models. The checker is kept small enough to be read and checked in full; Table 5.0a gives its size. A reader who doubts Proposition 1 can find in its output the specific record, month, and constraint at which plaintext semantics fails; a reader who doubts Proposition 2 can confirm that no violation arises under invalidation semantics across the generated instances.

old: The *realism layer* wraps the checker so that its inputs derive from Synthea-generated FHIR bundles rather than from abstract record identifiers, computing commitments over the actual payloads and constructing metadata from the actual encounter events. It is smaller than the checker (Table 5.0a) and is not load-bearing: if the wrapper were removed, the propositions and their executable check would stand unchanged. old: The proposition corrects as well as formalises. A collision needs a ceiling no longer than the floor whichever way it is anchored; what the anchor decides is whether the collision can be seen. A provision that measured both limits from one event and set the ceiling inside the floor would contradict itself on its face. Section 17 of politiregisterloven, a floor of twelve months and a ceiling of thirty-six from the same log entry, does not (Chapter 6, Section 6.9a). A ceiling measured from an external event can sit inside the floor with no visible contradiction, because whether the two clocks cross depends on when that event falls for each record. Article 68(12) is of the second kind: six months from permit expiry against twelve months from the log entry, with the collision arising for exactly the records whose permit expires within six months of the entry, which is the condition of Corollary 1.2. The diagnostic question for any candidate instance is therefore whether a ceiling no longer than the floor is anchored to an event other than the one the floor runs from.

old: *Key hierarchy.* Each record's payload is encrypted under a per-record data key $k(a)$. Per-record rather than per-subject or per-dataset granularity is required because the invalidation events of Proposition 2 occur at record granularity: a permit expiry invalidates the records of one permit, while an erasure request invalidates the records relating to one data subject, and these sets intersect without nesting. Data keys are themselves held under a key-encrypting key in a hardware security module or equivalent custody boundary. Destruction of $k(a)$ is effected by destruction of the wrapped data key and any cached copies, within the documented custody boundary. This is the hierarchy that key-management guidance prescribes, in which data keys are protected by key-encrypting keys and destruction means removing "all traces of a cryptographic key so that it cannot be recovered by either physical or electronic means" (Barker, 2020, Section 2.1). The optional module of the artefact executes it: per-record 256-bit data keys under AES in Galois/Counter Mode (Dworkin, 2007), each wrapped under a key-encrypting key and destroyed at the record's invalidation month (Appendix A, A.9e). The custody object stands in for a hardware security module, so destruction there is destruction in program memory.

old: *Tamper evidence.* An append-only registry is only as good as the means of detecting an append-only violation. Secure audit logging has addressed this since Schneier and Kelsey (1999), whose hash-chained logs make earlier entries unalterable without detection; Merkle trees (Merkle, 1988) let the same assurance be checked for a single entry with a logarithmic proof (Crosby & Wallach, 2009), and Certificate Transparency standardised that construction for public logs (Laurie, Langley, & Kasper, 2013). The mechanism appends every access event, invalidation and subject-link removal to such a log, with the leaf and node hashing of RFC 6962, and Semantics II condition (i) is checked as an inclusion proof against the log's root rather than as the presence of fields (Chapter 5, Section 5.6). What enters a leaf is chosen so that the log never needs erasing: the accessor fields, the creation month and the commitment, never the payload and never the subject fields. The tension that Chapter 2, Section 2.4 found unresolved in blockchain audit logging, an immutable trail facing an erasure right, therefore does not arise: what the right and the ceiling reach is held outside the log and destroyed there, and what the log holds is what accountability requires.

old: *Not established, and not claimed.* The demonstration does not prove the propositions for all instances; it checks them on the instances generated under one seed, and the exhaustive cross-check covers four small cases rather than the general result. The proofs in Chapter 4, not this chapter, carry the general claim. No performance measurement was taken, and no statement about execution time, throughput, or storage overhead appears anywhere in this thesis. The sandbox does not connect to any National Contact Point, implement the OpenNCP transmission flow, or evaluate consent policies. old: The sharpest instance is narrower, and rests on one contestable interpretive step. Article 73(1)(e) requires identifiable logs of access to and activity in a Secure Processing Environment to be kept for at least one year. Article 68(12) requires "the electronic health data within the secure processing environment" to be deleted within six months of the expiry of the data permit. Where an environment logs access at patient-record granularity, those log entries are electronic health data within the environment on the broad reading, and where the remaining permit duration at the time a log is written is six months or less, the two requirements overlap with no data subject acting. Chapter 4, Section 4.6 sets out the grounds on both sides. Chapter 5 produced thirty-nine witnesses of this collision in the model, in a population of one hundred Secure Processing Environment records; across the full population of two hundred, cross-border records included, ninety records were infeasible under Semantics I, most of them through erasure requests (Chapter 5, Table 5.1). Proposition 3 states the general condition: a ceiling no longer than the floor, anchored to an event other than the one the floor runs from. On the narrow reading, or where logs are kept at dataset granularity, the collision does not arise. On either reading the mechanism meets both provisions, because the accessor fields that Article 73(1)(e) requires to be identifiable are not the subject fields that Article 68(12) may reach.

old: The thesis's response is to be precise about what the invalidation entry is. It is an *attested* record of destruction, not a *proof* of it. The entry records that a named actor destroyed a named key at a named month on a named legal ground, and binds that claim into an append-only Merkle log alongside a commitment to the destroyed key's identifier, so that the claim, once made, cannot be altered or withdrawn without detection (Chapter 4, Section 4.8). Key-management guidance treats such a record as the normal trace of a destroyed key (Barker, 2020). An auditor can establish that the claim was made, by whom, and when; an auditor cannot establish that the claim is true. The difference between attestation and proof is the boundary of this contribution. Two things narrow it without closing it. Hardware security modules validated against FIPS 140-3 (National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2019) place destruction inside a tested boundary, though validation attests the design of the module, not any particular destruction. And the optional module of the artefact replaces the simulated key with real AES-256-GCM envelope encryption: after the 138 scheduled destructions, exactly those records refuse to decrypt (Chapter 5, Section 5.7), which shows that unreadability follows from the destruction, not that the destruction took place.

old: The first is the formalisation itself. Treating a retention conflict as a constraint-satisfaction problem over a single binary accessibility variable per record, and making the semantics of verifiability an explicit parameter of the model rather than an unexamined assumption, is a way of stating retention problems that appears not to have been used before in this domain. The general method of formalising legal compliance as satisfiability is established (Feng, Marsso, Sabetzadeh, & Chechik, 2023); its application here is what is new, and the applicability of the formulation beyond health data is an open question the thesis does not settle. The structure (one or more floors, a subject-triggered right, a ceiling) is not obviously specific to health. Section 6.9a tests that expectation against a statute outside health and returns a negative result which revises it: what matters is not that a floor and a ceiling coexist but where the ceiling is anchored. Financial record-keeping under MiFID II remains a candidate instance on that revised test, flagged for future analysis rather than established: the practitioner literature reviewed in Chapter 2 treats that setting as a floor-against-right conflict, and whether any ceiling analogous to Article 68(12) operates there is a question this thesis has not investigated.

old: *Feasibility results with an executable witness.* Proposition 1 establishes infeasibility under the status-quo semantics; Proposition 2 establishes satisfiability under the alternative and exhibits the trajectory that achieves it. old: *A mechanism specification with its residue analysed.* The mechanism applies established primitives (cryptographic erasure as recognised in NIST SP 800-88 Revision 2, hiding commitments, and, without implementing them, dynamic accumulators) and claims no cryptographic novelty. What it adds to the practitioner crypto-shredding pattern is verifiability: an auditor can establish what was invalidated, when, on what ground, and by whom, and can check each of those entries against the root of a Merkle log (Chapter 5, Section 5.6). The key hierarchy is executed with real AES-256-GCM in an optional module of the artefact. The residue it leaves is characterised as pseudonymised rather than anonymous by the Norwegian threshold, and designed to the corridor that the European Data Protection Board's finalised Guidelines 02/2025 establish.
